prompt: What makes a step idempotent?

choices.text: It never fails
choices.why: Failing has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: Running it twice leaves what running it once left
choices.why: Right. The same rows, the same values.

choices.text: It runs in one transaction from the first statement to the last
choices.why: A transaction can still insert the same rows twice.

choices.text: It is fast enough to run every night
choices.why: Speed is unrelated.

prompt: Which of these run a step more than once? Choose all that apply.
hint: The course has met all of them.

choices.text: A retry after a timeout
choices.why: Right. Lesson 10.

choices.text: Clearing a task days later
choices.why: Right. Lesson 10.

choices.text: A backfill over days already loaded
choices.why: Right. Lesson 9.

choices.text: A sensor that never pokes
choices.why: A sensor that never pokes runs nothing.

prompt: After the naive insert had run twice on top of the nightly, how many lines did the 16th have?
Why is a fingerprint better than a row count for comparing two runs?

choices.text: It is faster to compute
choices.why: It is slower; it reads every column.

choices.text: It ignores duplicate rows
choices.why: Duplicates change it.

choices.text: Any changed value changes it
choices.why: Right. A count only sees how many.

choices.text: PostgreSQL stores it with the table
choices.why: It is computed by the query.

prompt: Why does the fingerprint query sort the rows with `ORDER BY order_id, line_no`?

choices.text: So the same rows always give the same md5
choices.why: Right. Without an order, rows may come back in any order.

choices.text: To make the md5 faster to compute on a large day
choices.why: Order does not change the speed.

choices.text: To drop the duplicates
choices.why: ORDER BY removes nothing.

choices.text: Because string_agg refuses to run without an ORDER BY
choices.why: It is optional; leaving it out makes the result unstable.

prompt: What made `load/fact_sales.sql` idempotent?
hint: One line the naive load did not have.

choices.text: CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS
choices.why: That only creates the table once.

choices.text: psql's -q flag
choices.why: That only makes it quiet.

choices.text: A unique index on order_date
choices.why: There is none, and a day has many lines.

choices.text: It deletes the day first
choices.why: Right. It replaces the slice it owns.

prompt: Match each load to the idempotent shape it takes.
When is upsert the right shape?

choices.text: When rows arrive one by one, each with its own key
choices.why: Right. A second run finds every key and changes nothing.

choices.text: When a run owns a whole day
choices.why: That is delete then insert.

choices.text: When the table has no key
choices.why: Upsert needs a key.

choices.text: When the result is small enough to rebuild whole
choices.why: That is rebuild and swap.

prompt: What does `twice.sh` compare?

choices.text: The step's code as it was before and after the last edit
choices.why: It never reads the code.

choices.text: The exit codes
choices.why: set -e stops on a failure; the comparison is of the query.

choices.text: The time each run took, to see whether the second was faster
choices.why: Time is not compared.

choices.text: What the step left, after one run and after two
choices.why: Right. It tests the property, not the code.

prompt: A step inserts new prices, and `twice.sh` says it is idempotent on a day when the API returned nothing new. What has been shown?
hint: Did it have anything to write?

choices.text: That the step is idempotent
choices.why: Only that it wrote nothing twice.

choices.text: That the API is idempotent
choices.why: The API was not tested.

choices.text: Nothing useful: the test needs rows to write
choices.why: Right. Idempotent by luck is not idempotent.

choices.text: That the step is broken
choices.why: It did nothing wrong that day.

prompt: Why is `load_log` not idempotent, and why is that right?

choices.text: It is a bug; it should be fixed with an upsert
choices.why: Two loads happened, and it says so.

choices.text: It records runs, and two runs happened
choices.why: Right. A log is where appending is the point.

choices.text: now() is not allowed in PostgreSQL
choices.why: It is allowed; it differs each run.

choices.text: It has no primary key, so PostgreSQL cannot tell its rows apart
choices.why: A key would not change what it records.

prompt: Which of these break the idempotency of a table of facts about the shop? Choose all that apply.
hint: What differs from run to run?

choices.text: A column filled with now()
choices.why: Right. Every run writes a different value.

choices.text: An identity number used as a key elsewhere
choices.why: Right. Handed out in arrival order.

choices.text: random()
choices.why: Right. Different every time.

choices.text: A WHERE on the logical date
choices.why: The same run gives the same date.

prompt: How should an e-mail to the managers be made safe to run twice?
hint: It is an act, not a table.

choices.text: Make it an upsert
choices.why: An e-mail has no row to upsert.

choices.text: Retry it until the mail server answers and confirms that it delivered
choices.why: That is how it gets sent twice.

choices.text: Send it first, before the load runs, so a failure cannot send it twice
choices.why: It belongs at the end.

choices.text: Record that it was sent, and check that record before sending
choices.why: Right. A guard written on purpose.

prompt: The incremental model replaced only its newest day. Was it idempotent?
hint: Idempotent is not the same as complete.

choices.text: Yes, but older days could still change unseen
choices.why: Right. Idempotent, and incomplete.

choices.text: No, because it drifted
choices.why: Running it twice left the same table.

choices.text: No, because it used delete+insert
choices.why: That is what made it idempotent.

choices.text: Yes, and it was complete
choices.why: The drift test showed otherwise.

prompt: How many days back does the new `fact_sales` replace on every run?
What does the thirty-day window cost?

choices.text: Nothing at all
choices.why: Each run writes a month of lines.

choices.text: Each run writes about a month of lines instead of a day
choices.why: Right. Cheap here; real money on a large warehouse.

choices.text: The drift test can no longer run, since the window hides old days from it
choices.why: It runs and passes.

choices.text: Old days are deleted for good
choices.why: They are written again.

prompt: A window that each run deletes and writes again, to catch late changes, is called a ___.
hint: Lesson 4's word; how far back it looks.

prompt: What does *exactly once* mean in practice?

choices.text: A network that never loses or repeats a single message
choices.why: No network promises that.

choices.text: Never retrying a step
choices.why: Then things are lost.

choices.text: At least once, with idempotent writes
choices.why: Right. Nothing lost, duplicates harmless.

choices.text: Running everything once a day
choices.why: Frequency is not the point.

prompt: How does staging make a duplicated website event harmless?

choices.text: The collector stops sending duplicates
choices.why: It still sends them.

choices.text: It keeps one row per event_id
choices.why: Right. A second copy changes nothing.

choices.text: It deletes the day's file
choices.why: Files are kept.

choices.text: It counts events per session and drops the sessions with too many to be real
choices.why: Nothing is dropped by count.

prompt: Order the steps of `twice.sh`.
A backfill runs `load/fact_sales_append.sql` for the whole of March over days the nightly already loaded. What does the warehouse say about March afterwards?

choices.text: The right numbers, since the backfill reloaded them
choices.why: It added, it did not replace.

choices.text: The backfill fails on duplicate keys
choices.why: fact_sales has no unique key to stop it.

choices.text: Twice the sales, with no error anywhere
choices.why: Right. The most common silent failure.

choices.text: Only the newest day doubles
choices.why: Every day in the range does.
